notes: All 23 physical pages, three contact sheets, eight analytical figure/table objects, the contents roadmap, 29 retained/reconstructed formula interfaces, the two-page letter, and citations were inspected.
limitations: No watermark or AI Use Report is present.
All analytical figures and tables lack formal numbering/captions.
No code, appendix, raw data file, fitted-parameter ledger, or explicit temperature function is supplied.

task_reconstruction.objective: Estimate dragon growth, energy expenditure/intake, ecological and land requirements, climate effects, varying human assistance, reproduction, story guidance, and a real-world transfer.
inputs: official 10 kg and one-year mass facts plus narrative dragon traits
animal dimensions, metabolic references, activity multipliers
predator food/territory data, substrate water yields, cattle/farm averages
outputs: biome land area for one and three dragons
water requirement, dry-flight endurance, and temperature bounds
cow herd, pasture, direct labor, reproduction control, two-page letter, and real-world transfer
task_reconstruction.decision: Translate cross-scale biological and resource estimates into sustainable story and management guidance while preserving model-version and analogue boundaries.

section_map.summary: Six-paragraph executive ladder from scope through growth, calories, land, climate, and direct labor.
Conflicting feeding scenes motivate biological analogues rather than literal episode intake.
Four repeated objective lists route energy, land, climate, and intervention tasks.
Global and module-specific assumptions connect fiction to organism, predator, bird, and farm analogues.
Inline definitions bind growth, land, cow-rate, and labor symbols without a dedicated notation table.
Cubic scaling brackets Balerion before a modified von Bertalanffy age-mass curve is fitted.
Human-reference allometry is bounded, recalibrated to a whale, and multiplied by activity class.
Sustainability, water pathways, and maximum human provision decompose the resource problem.
Proxy calorie density, land division, cow cohorts, pasture, and labor form sequential arithmetic pipelines.
Narrative dimensions, episode rows, animal rates, biome proxies, water tables, and farm averages are selected.
Mass, calories, land, water endurance, herd, acreage, and labor outputs are reported in mixed numeric/symbolic form.
Controlled reproduction and conservation/agricultural transfer provide narrative closure.
Endpoint mass, territory, activity, and average-input assumptions are varied one at a time.
Scene, broad biological bounds, whale scale, and cross-biome tables provide internal plausibility checks.
Each model module names an analogue/data strength and a transfer, sensitivity, feasibility, or ethics limitation.
Measurement, prey composition, and distributed logistics are named as concrete extensions.
A two-page letter compresses food, arid travel, temperature, conservation, and agriculture into story guidance.

contributions.summary: Combines two physical analogues with a modified von Bertalanffy curve to create an age-indexed mass state.
Uses a broad biological bound and a whale recalibration before translating demand into cows.
Builds a six-biome proxy table from apex-predator food and territory data.
Separates arid metabolic water from temperature-driven activity bounds.
Constructs a symbolic cow, pasture, and direct-labor pipeline for full human provision.
Translates the model chain into a two-page audience-specific recommendation.

edges.handoff: The two-analogue mass estimate supplies the upper-mass anchor Winf.
The fitted age-mass curve supplies W(t) to human-reference allometry.
The human-reference coefficient is challenged and superseded by the blue-whale calibration.
Revised basal calories should supply the activity multiplier interface.
Alternative Balerion masses trigger refitted growth curves.
Very-active daily calories should feed the land numerator, although the paper reverts to the old coefficient.
The age-nine mass and calorie state supplies the water-scene calibration.
Sedentary/light activity calories supply the claimed daily water need.
Activity multipliers define the proposed temperature asymptotes.
Water and temperature are presented as the two climate-response branches.
Daily calorie demand should close x cows/day, but the paper leaves the handoff symbolic.
The three-dragon herd H3 supplies the pasture and labor calculation.
Land/resource limits are invoked as a future dragon carrying capacity.
Human provisioning limits are also invoked for population control.

assumptions.summary: Dragons can be biologically compared with existing animals and modeled uniformly.
Flight existence is accepted as a premise.
Dragons have indeterminate growth, a roughly 250-year maximum age, and Balerion is near the size limit.
Red meat/fish can meet calories without nutrition modeling.
Natural apex-predator intake is sustainable and transferable to dragons.
Dragon calories are temporarily constant across biomes and hunting is very active.
Migratory birds proxy dragon climate behavior and prey is the normal water source.
One human supplies exactly one day of water with complete extraction.
Activity changes regulate environmental temperature effects.
Dragons can bond new riders and optimized farms avoid drought.
Any pair can reproduce and eggs can be stored until controlled hatching.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: 42-50 m length and 150 m wingspan estimates for Balerion.
Pterosaur 9 m/250 kg and Komodo 3 m/70 kg endpoints.
Eight episode-age-size rows plus selected 5 kg, 30 kg, and 219,901 kg anchors.
Human 100 kg reference, quarter-power law, elephant comparison.
0.3-9 W/kg range and 173 tonne blue-whale reference.
Food mass and territories for wolf, tiger, lynx, coyote, lion, and arctic wolf proxies.
Fat and protein energy/water yields copied from a cited bird paper.
71,799 kcal, 81,000 kcal human food value, 62 kg mass, and 90% assumed water.
2,000 lb cow, 8,000 lb/acre yield, 445 acre farm, 1.38 workers/farm.

verification.summary: The printed fitted curve approximately reproduces its three selected anchors.
The whale-calibrated demand is placed inside a broad vertebrate rate interval.
Age-nine demand is compared with a human-feeding scene.
Low/high analogue masses are plotted around the central curve.
Territory and activity endpoints are propagated one factor at a time.
Assimilation and scene-adequacy assumptions are explicitly identified as uncertain.
Drought, average inputs, and imperfect cow replacement are identified as upward biases.
Ethics and land concentration are separated from mathematical feasibility.
The letter repeats central body outputs and real-world transfers.

results_trace.summary: 710.8 square miles per Balerion-sized dragon and 2,132.4 for three.
292.5 square miles in savannah to 7,108.2 in arctic tundra per dragon.
49.46 kg/day and 7.5 hours claimed dry-flight endurance.
Egg collection proposed as a population-control mechanism.
Conservation resource adequacy and agricultural burden are proposed applications.

writing_logic.summary: Scope -> growth -> calories -> land -> climate -> intervention.
Each module opens with aims and assumptions before method.
Two scaled organisms bound the historical maximum used by growth.
A human-reference result is challenged by bounds and recalibrated to a whale.
Calories feed biome density division and land.
The constant-climate simplification is retired before water and temperature branches.
Daily cows feed herd, pasture, farms, and direct workers.
Core outputs are compressed into story and conservation guidance.

language_observations.summary: Reusable move: whole-paper scope and modeling ladder; order fictional system -> realistic concerns -> modeling ladder; boundary: A scope paragraph should expose the full analytical ladder rather than only the theme.

Reusable move: analogue-to-growth-equation capsule; order largest analogue -> scaled estimate -> growth family -> trajectory output; boundary: An abstract model claim needs the analogue and fitted state, not an unsupported accuracy adjective.

Reusable move: multi-route calorie selection capsule; order candidate methods -> plausibility comparison -> selected calibration -> interpretable food unit; boundary: A multi-route claim should state the selection criterion and final unit-bearing result.

Reusable move: apex-predator land transfer capsule; order biome analogue -> prey calorie density -> dragon demand -> land requirement; boundary: A cross-species transfer must retain whether the analogue is an individual, group, or displaced incumbent.

Reusable move: climate split and endurance result; order climate drivers -> metabolic-water bridge -> temperature behavior -> endurance output; boundary: A climate capsule should show how each driver reconnects to resource demand.

Reusable move: symbolic community result; order food production -> farm labor -> riders and safety -> community expression; boundary: A symbolic result must define its free variable correctly and distinguish direct labor from total community size.

Reusable move: narrative anomaly to biological model; order conflicting observations -> measurement problem -> analogue choice; boundary: A narrative anomaly should motivate a measurable substitute rather than erase the contradiction.

Reusable move: contrasting episode evidence; order observed feeding -> speaker interpretation -> later counterexample -> modeling need; boundary: Episode evidence remains qualitative unless intake, interval, and animal state are identified.
Reusable move: fiction-to-analogue handoff; order fictional uncertainty -> real organism class -> transfer boundary; boundary: The analogue class must be justified by the mechanism being transferred.

Reusable move: energy objective checklist; order basal demand -> activity expenditure -> climate effect; boundary: An objective list should map each promised output to a later equation or explicit omission.
Reusable move: two-stage land objective; order sustainable density -> dragon calorie demand -> area division; boundary: A land objective should preserve the time unit and sustainability definition.

Reusable move: two-factor climate objective; order temperature -> water scarcity -> resource consequence; boundary: A climate objective needs a quantitative driver-response interface for every listed factor.

Reusable move: intervention objective split; order control labor -> food labor -> community output; boundary: An intervention objective must distinguish direct staff, supply-chain labor, and community population.

Reusable move: analogue assumption with justification; order fictional gap -> physical basis -> Earth analogue; boundary: A transfer assumption should identify the specific conserved mechanism and its scale limit.

Reusable move: given-function boundary; order official premise -> accepted function -> retained physical accounting; boundary: Accepting flight does not remove the need to account for its energy and resource consequences.

Reusable move: thermoregulation classification; order observed heat trait -> classification -> metabolic implication; boundary: A biological classification should remain consistent with later behavioral analogues.

Reusable move: natural-predator sustainability proxy; order observed predator -> assumed equilibrium -> dragon transfer; boundary: A sustainability proxy must state whether the new consumer replaces or adds to existing predators.

Reusable move: scene-derived water calibration; order scene intake -> daily adequacy assumption -> water extraction assumption -> calibration point; boundary: A scene-derived calibration must expose efficiency and adequacy uncertainty.
Reusable move: equation-following symbol ledger; order symbol -> quantity -> unit -> scope; boundary: A symbol ledger must include the time base and avoid reuse for a different mass.
Reusable move: output definition after equation; order output symbol -> resource purpose -> inherited inputs; boundary: An output definition should repeat units when upstream notation is overloaded.

Reusable move: free-variable declaration before pipeline; order free variable -> per-dragon rate -> time unit -> pipeline consumer; boundary: A free variable must be numerically closed before downstream totals are presented as answers.

Reusable move: cubic similitude bridge; order reference length -> scale ratio -> uniform density -> mass estimate; boundary: Cubic scaling requires one consistent characteristic length and a checked exponent calculation.

Reusable move: bracket then average; order light flying analogue -> dense terrestrial analogue -> bracket -> central estimate; boundary: Averaging analogues is defensible only after arithmetic and weighting rationale are stated.

Reusable move: reject point-only interpolation; order candidate fit -> physical objection -> source chronology issue -> mechanistic model; boundary: Rejecting interpolation should be followed by a transparent retained-data ledger.

Reusable move: candidate-family comparison; order growth requirement -> candidate families -> limit behavior -> selected family; boundary: Model selection must reconcile the stated limiting behavior with the selected equation.

Reusable move: length-to-mass transformation; order length law -> volume relation -> mass law -> parameter interpretation; boundary: A transformed model should declare the density coefficient and dimensional consistency.

Reusable move: anchor-to-curve handoff; order selected anchors -> parameter fit -> curve -> later consumer; boundary: Reliability language should name which points were retained and how the parameters were solved.

Reusable move: size-dependent specific metabolism; order mass effect -> specific rate -> total demand; boundary: Allometric scaling must preserve the reference mass and coefficient through composition.
Reusable move: mouse-elephant intuition; order small-animal contrast -> large-animal contrast -> scaling law; boundary: An intuition example should not substitute for a scale-matched calibration.

Reusable move: biological range before calibration; order broad vertebrate range -> heat plausibility -> reference animal -> selected estimate; boundary: A bound must be converted with the correct units before it is used as validation.

Reusable move: near-scale reference update; order reference mismatch -> blue-whale rate -> new coefficient -> revised demand; boundary: Once a coefficient is superseded, every downstream consumer must use the revised version.

Reusable move: activity multiplier bridge; order basal demand -> activity class -> multiplier -> daily intake; boundary: A human activity multiplier should be labeled as an analogy and tested against flight-specific expenditure.

Reusable move: operational sustainability definition; order resource condition -> regeneration condition -> permanent-damage boundary; boundary: A sustainability definition needs a time horizon and coupled incumbent demand.

Reusable move: natural-balance reasoning; order existing predator -> territory -> daily food -> calorie density; boundary: Observed range size is not automatically a direct estimator of prey production.

Reusable move: constant-demand assumption retired; order previous simplification -> environmental behavior -> caloric correction -> resource feedback; boundary: A retired assumption must trigger recomputation in dependent models.
Reusable move: dual water-source decomposition; order prey water -> metabolic water -> arid shift -> storage limit; boundary: A dual-source ledger must keep mass, energy, and time units consistent.

Reusable move: maximum-intervention scenario; order all food supplied -> cow pipeline -> land -> labor; boundary: One maximum-assistance scenario does not answer varying assistance levels without a scenario parameter.

Reusable move: derive density then divide demand; order predator food mass -> calories per pound -> territory -> density -> dragon demand -> area; boundary: The algorithm must preserve day in the density unit and use the current demand equation.

Reusable move: conservative upper-state calculation; order largest reference dragon -> risk of hunger -> upper area; boundary: A conservative bound should distinguish three actual dragons from three copies of the historical maximum.

Reusable move: steady-throughput cohort construction; order daily cow demand -> calving interval -> maturation lag -> breeder stock -> immature stock; boundary: A cohort pipeline must separate cycle time from maturation delay and account for age structure.

Reusable move: land-to-farm-to-worker conversion; order acre requirement -> average farm size -> workers per farm -> riders -> security; boundary: Direct labor should not be relabeled as total community population.

Reusable move: two-source scale inputs; order reference dimensions -> reference mass -> target dimension -> scaled mass; boundary: Every endpoint should retain source, characteristic length, and arithmetic trace.
Reusable move: plot-driven data correction; order episode table -> chronology concern -> adjustment rule -> retained anchors; boundary: Adjusted data must be published rather than only described.

Reusable move: mean-of-range preprocessing; order source range -> mean rule -> table value -> sensitivity endpoints; boundary: A mean should be accompanied by the original range and weighting assumptions.
Reusable move: source table ingestion; order substrate rows -> energy basis -> water basis -> citation; boundary: A copied table must preserve original units and conversion direction.
Reusable move: analogue average result; order two estimates -> central mass -> reference comparison; boundary: A central result should not survive a failed endpoint calculation without correction.

Reusable move: growth-to-demand checkpoint; order age -> mass -> basal calories -> scene comparison; boundary: A checkpoint should specify whether a time-skip adjustment is actually encoded in the equation.
Reusable move: calorie-to-cow translation; order revised BMR -> adult mass -> cow calories -> food count; boundary: A food result must state whether it is basal or activity-adjusted.

Reusable move: unit-bearing area answer; order daily demand -> calorie density -> one-dragon area -> three-dragon area; boundary: A land result must identify the demand coefficient and whether incumbents remain.

Reusable move: metabolic-water ratio to duration; order water need -> metabolic yield -> relative depletion -> flight duration; boundary: An endurance result requires a valid kJ-kcal conversion and reserve-capacity model.
Reusable move: symbolic staffing output; order farm workers -> riders -> security midpoint -> symbolic total; boundary: A symbolic result is incomplete until x is evaluated for a named dragon state.

Reusable move: control-oriented population conclusion; order egg storage -> hatching trigger -> carrying capacity -> population control; boundary: A control conclusion needs a capacity estimate and failure scenario.

Reusable move: fiction-to-conservation transfer; order animal demand model -> ecosystem adequacy -> at-risk species -> resource targeting; boundary: Transfer claims require recalibration and measured ecosystem data.

Reusable move: resource-pressure reframing; order cow pipeline -> human demand -> environmental burden -> awareness; boundary: A rhetorical transfer should distinguish illustrative accounting from validated policy analysis.
Reusable move: endpoint sweep; order low analogue -> central analogue -> high analogue -> growth curves; boundary: Sensitivity equations must reproduce the endpoint assumptions and plotted signs.
Reusable move: scale-error propagation; order length uncertainty -> cubic mass -> calorie propagation; boundary: A qualitative amplification claim should report numerical output elasticity.
Reusable move: input-range propagation; order territory endpoints -> calorie-density endpoints -> land effect; boundary: One-factor endpoints are interpretation, not joint robustness.

Reusable move: assumption inventory; order input averages -> drought boundary -> pipeline imperfection -> direction of bias; boundary: A sensitivity inventory should quantify the final staffing and land response.

Reusable move: internal scene plausibility check; order predicted calories -> human calories -> activity -> qualitative scene; boundary: A fictional scene is an internal plausibility check, not external validation.
Reusable move: scale-matched benchmark; order nearby mass scale -> reported daily energy -> new coefficient; boundary: A benchmark requires the correct citation and comparable activity/physiology.
Reusable move: selected estimate inside broad range; order broad bound -> selected value -> plausibility conclusion; boundary: Being inside a broad range does not establish predictive accuracy.
Reusable move: scenario-table comparison; order biome -> predator proxy -> density -> area rank; boundary: A comparison table should keep entity definitions and units consistent across rows.
Reusable move: candidate-model comparison strength; order candidate methods -> plausibility criteria -> selected analogue; boundary: A claimed strength should identify the actual comparison evidence.
Reusable move: real-ecosystem basis strength; order observed predators -> territory -> food -> transfer; boundary: Real-world inputs do not make a cross-scale model validated by themselves.

Reusable move: added-load limitation; order replacement assumption -> incumbent demand -> prey regeneration gap; boundary: A limitation should be propagated into the result boundary, not left as prose only.

Reusable move: implementation and ethics boundary; order optimized farm -> animal welfare -> land concentration -> applicability; boundary: Ethical feasibility is distinct from arithmetic resource feasibility.
Reusable move: measurement plan; order future observations -> model comparison -> parameter update; boundary: A measurement plan should specify frequency, uncertainty, and holdout use.

Reusable move: prey-composition extension; order diet composition -> incumbent predators -> regeneration -> joint demand; boundary: An extension should name the additional state variables and validation data.

Reusable move: distributed supply-chain extension; order multiple farms -> transport -> labor -> losses; boundary: A distributed extension should add logistics costs rather than only relax co-location.
Reusable move: audience-purpose opening; order recipient -> purpose -> credibility -> story value; boundary: A stakeholder letter should lead with the decision and avoid overstating rigor.
Reusable move: source assumptions before guidance; order diet -> growth -> analogue -> calorie model; boundary: A letter should distinguish source facts from added assumptions.
Reusable move: quantified story guidance; order largest dragon -> food count -> recommendation; boundary: A recommendation must carry the same activity state as its source calculation.

Reusable move: threshold recommendation; order arid condition -> metabolic water -> duration -> provisioning action; boundary: A threshold recommendation should state uncertainty and the calculation boundary.

Reusable move: explicit transfer boundary; order fiction caveat -> animal model -> conservation use -> recalibration; boundary: A transfer paragraph must not imply that fictional calibration is directly operational.

Reusable move: respectful implementation close; order analysis recap -> implementation request -> audience close; boundary: A closing should repeat the highest-priority executable guidance, not only goodwill.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A complete model ladder and unit-bearing headline results improve first-pass traceability; this paper's symbolic community result remains underclosed.
Cross-biome comparability is useful only when entity definitions, time units, and model versions remain consistent.
Climate analysis should reconnect water and temperature outputs to the food, land, and community decisions.
Audience guidance should preserve the same model version, activity state, and uncertainty as the body.

weaknesses.summary: The official problem states a roughly 10 kg hatch mass and asks teams to assume that basic biology is accurate, but the paper replaces it with 5 kg because the authors prefer a bat analogy.

The energy model uses BMR plus human activity multipliers and never separately accounts for long-distance flight, fire breathing, trauma resistance, hunting mechanics, thermoregulation, or reproduction.
Balerion is first described as roughly 42 m long and then scaled as 50 m long from crocodile teeth without reconciling which length drives mass.
Scaling a 250 kg, 9 m-wingspan pterosaur to 150 m by the paper's cubic law gives about 1,157,407 kg, not 115,740 kg; the printed estimate is low by a factor of ten.
Correcting the pterosaur endpoint makes the mean of the pterosaur and Komodo estimates about 740,741 kg rather than 219,901 kg, changing every downstream upper-state result.
The model-selection prose says dragons grow without limit and therefore should not have an asymptote, but it selects a von Bertalanffy model with finite L_inf and W_inf.
The condition d^2y/dx^2 < 1 does not define attenuating unbounded growth; concavity would require a sign comparison with zero and still would not guarantee an unbounded function.
Citation [24] is used to support von Bertalanffy or indeterminate growth, but reference [24] is a Smithsonian Komodo-dragon page; the indeterminate-growth item is [25].
The episode table assigns 2.5 years to both 3 ft and 7 ft and 3 years to both 12 ft and 25 ft; the paper says points were adjusted but never publishes the adjusted dataset or fit ledger.
The final growth equation mixes x inside an equation defined as W(t), leaving the age symbol inconsistent across the model and later evaluations.
t0 is described as the t value such that W(t)=5, but in the equation it is a shift parameter; t0=1.203 makes W(0) about 5 rather than W(1.203)=5.
After deriving B=65.3M^-0.25 from the 100 kg reference, the age-composed line prints B(t)=20.65W(t)^-0.25 and silently drops the reference-mass factor.
The stated 0.3-9 W/kg range converts to about 6.20-185.85 kcal/(kg day), not 3-92; the conversion is approximately one-half of the correct range.
At 219,901 kg and 500,000 kcal per cow, the corrected broad rate range is about 2.72-81.74 cows/day, not 1.32-40.46.
The blue-whale daily-energy statement cites [25], which is an indeterminate-growth source; [26] discusses calories swallowed in one mouthful and does not directly establish daily BMR.
57,728 multiplied by the lightly-active factor 1.375 is about 79,376, not 74,324; the captive activity interval is understated.
The midpoint of the correct sedentary-to-light interval is about 74,325, not 71,799; the erroneous value is reused in the water model.
The calorie-over-time graph plateaus near 2.3e5 kcal/day, while the revised formula C=177.4W^0.75 approaches about 1.82e6 kcal/day at W_inf; the graph appears to use an older coefficient.
The low-mass sensitivity equation is visually printed with a positive exponent, producing large negative mass after cubing rather than the plotted positive saturating curve.
The high-mass sensitivity equation is also visually printed with a positive exponent and cannot generate the displayed positive saturating curve.
The sensitivity plot evidently uses negative exponents while both displayed formulas use positive exponents, so the figure and equation interfaces disagree.
Even restoring negative signs to the rounded low/high equations yields age-220 masses around 117,102 and 313,702 kg, not exactly the asserted 115,740 and 324,074 kg endpoints.
The proposed food/space extension only lowers W_inf; without refitting K and t0 this also changes birth and one-year mass rather than isolating an adult resource limit.
The land model reverts to C=65.3W^0.75 after the paper supersedes it with C=177.4W^0.75, understating every land result by about 2.7167.
Using the revised coefficient and the paper's same biome densities gives about 5,793 square miles for three dragons in temperate forest and 57,933 in arctic tundra, not 2,132.4 and 21,324.7.
N is described and tabled as calories per square mile, but because food intake is daily its unit is kcal/(day square mile); the missing time unit obscures dimensional closure.
W denotes dragon mass in the growth and metabolic models but denotes predator food weight in the land equation, creating a cross-model symbol collision.
The paper cites [6] for a universal 1490 kcal/lb meat conversion, but [6] concerns metabolic scaling rather than meat energy density.
Wolf and likely lion rows use group-level food and territory while other rows appear individual; the entity level is not defined consistently across biomes.
The model treats dragon intake as replacing a natural apex predator rather than adding a new consumer; the authors acknowledge this only after reporting area results.
Ecological impact is not quantitatively modeled beyond proxy land: fire, species loss, competition, waste, water depletion, methane, and incumbent predator effects remain qualitative.
The weighted metabolic-water yield is 0.0508 g/kJ; converting to per kcal requires multiplication by 4.184, giving about 0.21255 g/kcal rather than the paper's 0.086.
Using the paper's 0.689 g/kcal water need and corrected 0.21255 g/kcal metabolic yield gives a multiplier about 3.24 and roughly 18.5 hours, not 7.5 hours.
Dividing kg/day by kcal/day yields g/kcal; the paper retains an extra /day in its normalized water-intensity unit.
0.689 g/kcal equals 0.000689 L/kcal, not 0.00689 L/kcal; the freshwater conversion is high by a factor of ten.
The printed freshwater intensity implies about 494.7 L/day at 71,799 kcal, contradicting the same page's 49.46 kg/day water requirement.
The human is assumed to be 90% water and all 55.8 kg is treated as available, despite no source or body-composition boundary for that value.
One feeding scene is assumed to provide exactly one day of both calories and water with 100% extraction efficiency; adequacy and assimilation are unobserved.
A 2.5-day bird migration is shortened linearly by a water-yield ratio without showing comparable fat/protein reserve mass, dehydration threshold, flight power, or body scaling for dragons.
Water need is calibrated from sedentary/light activity calories and then applied to continuous flight, so the activity state changes between calibration and use.
57,728 multiplied by 1.2 is 69,273.6, not the printed 69,264 kcal/day.

The paragraph says hot conditions induce rest and cold conditions induce more activity, but its final sentence says calorie demand grows with larger temperature values; Summary and letter say cold demand is higher.
The claimed temperature logistic model has no equation, temperature unit, direction, midpoint, slope, data, figure, or fitting rule; two horizontal bounds do not identify it.
Neither the water nor temperature correction is propagated back into biome land, cow demand, farm area, or community labor, so the climate branch does not close the resource chain.
The paper's own timings imply a repeat calving interval near 283+55=338 days; adding the 730-day maturation lag to obtain 1068 breeder cows confuses throughput cycle with pipeline delay.
The 730-day maturation delay is included once in the 1068x breeder count and again as 730x immature cows, double-counting the same delay.
The cow pipeline does not explicitly close sex ratio, failed pregnancies, calf mortality, nonbreeding age, replacement timing, or whether every carcass remains nutritionally usable.
All 5394x cattle, including immature cohorts, are assigned a 2,000 lb adult weight and 4% daily forage intake, inconsistent with the paper's own age structure.
x is never evaluated from C(t)/500000 for a named dragon age and activity state, so actual herd, acre, and people totals are never produced.
Summary defines x as the amount of people per day, while section 6.3 defines x as cows required per dragon per day.
61x+48 includes only direct farm workers, three riders, and average security; it is not a total community size and omits households, logistics, machinery, veterinary care, and services.
The claim that high body temperature prevents any disease, analogized to bats, is uncited and biologically absolute.
The reproduction section says prior models can find carrying capacity but never computes it or supplies egg production, hatching, mortality, or a population trajectory.
The inference that dragons can mate regardless of genetic relation because humans in the story accept incest does not provide biological evidence about dragon reproduction.
The letter calls Rhaegal 'Rhaegar,' changing the named dragon.
The letter says dragons grow indefinitely, while the body explicitly uses a finite W_inf von Bertalanffy curve.
The letter presents 3.6 cows/day as the largest-dragon food limit, but 3.6 is basal demand; the paper's own multipliers imply at least 4.32 sedentary and about 6.21 very-active cows/day.
The assumptions say dragons need red meat and red meat alone, immediately say they can also eat fish, and the letter changes the claim to meat and fish without reconciling nutrition.
The paper classifies dragons as endotherms but later justifies temperature behavior using reptilian behavioral thermoregulation without explaining how the mechanisms combine.
The required letter discusses arid and cold/arctic conditions but gives almost no warm-temperate comparison or quantitative migration resource change.
The official varying-assistance requirement is reduced to one 100% human-provision scenario; partial hunting is mentioned only qualitatively and no assistance parameter or scenario table is supplied.
Three-dragon land is computed as three copies of Balerion rather than using the ages and masses of the three living dragons or showing land growth over time.
Summary reports no land-area number, no evaluated community population, and no final growth formula; its only community expression also defines x incorrectly.
The three growth sensitivity curves have no legend, so low, central, and high cases cannot be identified from the figure alone.
The paper's analytical figures and tables have no Figure/Table numbers or formal captions; the growth input table also lacks source-to-row labeling.
The episode size table is not connected to a transparent retained-versus-adjusted flag, so a reader cannot reproduce which rows informed the final curve.

independent_extensions.summary: Refit growth with the official 10 kg anchor, corrected cubic scaling, explicit retained data, residuals, and model-family comparison.
Create a versioned W(t)->BMR->activity pipeline and prohibit downstream use of superseded coefficients.
Replace range-area proxying with prey productivity, incumbent predators, seasonal regeneration, and dragon diet composition.
Build a mass-energy-water balance with reserve mass, flight power, dehydration threshold, and correct unit conversions.
Fit an explicit temperature response and propagate it through calories, land, water, cows, and labor.
Define an assistance fraction from self-hunting to full provision and solve multiple community scenarios.
Use an age-structured, sex-structured cattle pipeline with calving interval, maturation delay, mortality, and transport.
Quantify ecological impact from fire, predation, competition, water withdrawal, waste, methane, and population growth.

unresolved_questions.summary: The official problem states a roughly 10 kg hatch mass and asks teams to assume that basic biology is accurate, but the paper replaces it with 5 kg because the authors prefer a bat analogy.

The energy model uses BMR plus human activity multipliers and never separately accounts for long-distance flight, fire breathing, trauma resistance, hunting mechanics, thermoregulation, or reproduction.
Balerion is first described as roughly 42 m long and then scaled as 50 m long from crocodile teeth without reconciling which length drives mass.
Scaling a 250 kg, 9 m-wingspan pterosaur to 150 m by the paper's cubic law gives about 1,157,407 kg, not 115,740 kg; the printed estimate is low by a factor of ten.
Correcting the pterosaur endpoint makes the mean of the pterosaur and Komodo estimates about 740,741 kg rather than 219,901 kg, changing every downstream upper-state result.
The model-selection prose says dragons grow without limit and therefore should not have an asymptote, but it selects a von Bertalanffy model with finite L_inf and W_inf.
The condition d^2y/dx^2 < 1 does not define attenuating unbounded growth; concavity would require a sign comparison with zero and still would not guarantee an unbounded function.
Citation [24] is used to support von Bertalanffy or indeterminate growth, but reference [24] is a Smithsonian Komodo-dragon page; the indeterminate-growth item is [25].
The episode table assigns 2.5 years to both 3 ft and 7 ft and 3 years to both 12 ft and 25 ft; the paper says points were adjusted but never publishes the adjusted dataset or fit ledger.
The final growth equation mixes x inside an equation defined as W(t), leaving the age symbol inconsistent across the model and later evaluations.
t0 is described as the t value such that W(t)=5, but in the equation it is a shift parameter; t0=1.203 makes W(0) about 5 rather than W(1.203)=5.
After deriving B=65.3M^-0.25 from the 100 kg reference, the age-composed line prints B(t)=20.65W(t)^-0.25 and silently drops the reference-mass factor.
The stated 0.3-9 W/kg range converts to about 6.20-185.85 kcal/(kg day), not 3-92; the conversion is approximately one-half of the correct range.
At 219,901 kg and 500,000 kcal per cow, the corrected broad rate range is about 2.72-81.74 cows/day, not 1.32-40.46.
The blue-whale daily-energy statement cites [25], which is an indeterminate-growth source; [26] discusses calories swallowed in one mouthful and does not directly establish daily BMR.
57,728 multiplied by the lightly-active factor 1.375 is about 79,376, not 74,324; the captive activity interval is understated.
The midpoint of the correct sedentary-to-light interval is about 74,325, not 71,799; the erroneous value is reused in the water model.
The calorie-over-time graph plateaus near 2.3e5 kcal/day, while the revised formula C=177.4W^0.75 approaches about 1.82e6 kcal/day at W_inf; the graph appears to use an older coefficient.
The low-mass sensitivity equation is visually printed with a positive exponent, producing large negative mass after cubing rather than the plotted positive saturating curve.
The high-mass sensitivity equation is also visually printed with a positive exponent and cannot generate the displayed positive saturating curve.
The sensitivity plot evidently uses negative exponents while both displayed formulas use positive exponents, so the figure and equation interfaces disagree.
Even restoring negative signs to the rounded low/high equations yields age-220 masses around 117,102 and 313,702 kg, not exactly the asserted 115,740 and 324,074 kg endpoints.
The proposed food/space extension only lowers W_inf; without refitting K and t0 this also changes birth and one-year mass rather than isolating an adult resource limit.
The land model reverts to C=65.3W^0.75 after the paper supersedes it with C=177.4W^0.75, understating every land result by about 2.7167.
Using the revised coefficient and the paper's same biome densities gives about 5,793 square miles for three dragons in temperate forest and 57,933 in arctic tundra, not 2,132.4 and 21,324.7.
N is described and tabled as calories per square mile, but because food intake is daily its unit is kcal/(day square mile); the missing time unit obscures dimensional closure.
W denotes dragon mass in the growth and metabolic models but denotes predator food weight in the land equation, creating a cross-model symbol collision.
The paper cites [6] for a universal 1490 kcal/lb meat conversion, but [6] concerns metabolic scaling rather than meat energy density.
Wolf and likely lion rows use group-level food and territory while other rows appear individual; the entity level is not defined consistently across biomes.
The model treats dragon intake as replacing a natural apex predator rather than adding a new consumer; the authors acknowledge this only after reporting area results.
Ecological impact is not quantitatively modeled beyond proxy land: fire, species loss, competition, waste, water depletion, methane, and incumbent predator effects remain qualitative.
The weighted metabolic-water yield is 0.0508 g/kJ; converting to per kcal requires multiplication by 4.184, giving about 0.21255 g/kcal rather than the paper's 0.086.
Using the paper's 0.689 g/kcal water need and corrected 0.21255 g/kcal metabolic yield gives a multiplier about 3.24 and roughly 18.5 hours, not 7.5 hours.
Dividing kg/day by kcal/day yields g/kcal; the paper retains an extra /day in its normalized water-intensity unit.
0.689 g/kcal equals 0.000689 L/kcal, not 0.00689 L/kcal; the freshwater conversion is high by a factor of ten.
The printed freshwater intensity implies about 494.7 L/day at 71,799 kcal, contradicting the same page's 49.46 kg/day water requirement.
The human is assumed to be 90% water and all 55.8 kg is treated as available, despite no source or body-composition boundary for that value.
One feeding scene is assumed to provide exactly one day of both calories and water with 100% extraction efficiency; adequacy and assimilation are unobserved.
A 2.5-day bird migration is shortened linearly by a water-yield ratio without showing comparable fat/protein reserve mass, dehydration threshold, flight power, or body scaling for dragons.
Water need is calibrated from sedentary/light activity calories and then applied to continuous flight, so the activity state changes between calibration and use.
57,728 multiplied by 1.2 is 69,273.6, not the printed 69,264 kcal/day.

The paragraph says hot conditions induce rest and cold conditions induce more activity, but its final sentence says calorie demand grows with larger temperature values; Summary and letter say cold demand is higher.
The claimed temperature logistic model has no equation, temperature unit, direction, midpoint, slope, data, figure, or fitting rule; two horizontal bounds do not identify it.
Neither the water nor temperature correction is propagated back into biome land, cow demand, farm area, or community labor, so the climate branch does not close the resource chain.
The paper's own timings imply a repeat calving interval near 283+55=338 days; adding the 730-day maturation lag to obtain 1068 breeder cows confuses throughput cycle with pipeline delay.
The 730-day maturation delay is included once in the 1068x breeder count and again as 730x immature cows, double-counting the same delay.
The cow pipeline does not explicitly close sex ratio, failed pregnancies, calf mortality, nonbreeding age, replacement timing, or whether every carcass remains nutritionally usable.
All 5394x cattle, including immature cohorts, are assigned a 2,000 lb adult weight and 4% daily forage intake, inconsistent with the paper's own age structure.
x is never evaluated from C(t)/500000 for a named dragon age and activity state, so actual herd, acre, and people totals are never produced.
Summary defines x as the amount of people per day, while section 6.3 defines x as cows required per dragon per day.
61x+48 includes only direct farm workers, three riders, and average security; it is not a total community size and omits households, logistics, machinery, veterinary care, and services.
The claim that high body temperature prevents any disease, analogized to bats, is uncited and biologically absolute.
The reproduction section says prior models can find carrying capacity but never computes it or supplies egg production, hatching, mortality, or a population trajectory.
The inference that dragons can mate regardless of genetic relation because humans in the story accept incest does not provide biological evidence about dragon reproduction.
The letter calls Rhaegal 'Rhaegar,' changing the named dragon.
The letter says dragons grow indefinitely, while the body explicitly uses a finite W_inf von Bertalanffy curve.
The letter presents 3.6 cows/day as the largest-dragon food limit, but 3.6 is basal demand; the paper's own multipliers imply at least 4.32 sedentary and about 6.21 very-active cows/day.
The assumptions say dragons need red meat and red meat alone, immediately say they can also eat fish, and the letter changes the claim to meat and fish without reconciling nutrition.
The paper classifies dragons as endotherms but later justifies temperature behavior using reptilian behavioral thermoregulation without explaining how the mechanisms combine.
The required letter discusses arid and cold/arctic conditions but gives almost no warm-temperate comparison or quantitative migration resource change.
The official varying-assistance requirement is reduced to one 100% human-provision scenario; partial hunting is mentioned only qualitatively and no assistance parameter or scenario table is supplied.
Three-dragon land is computed as three copies of Balerion rather than using the ages and masses of the three living dragons or showing land growth over time.
Summary reports no land-area number, no evaluated community population, and no final growth formula; its only community expression also defines x incorrectly.
The three growth sensitivity curves have no legend, so low, central, and high cases cannot be identified from the figure alone.
